For lower- voltage facilities—defined as facilities operating below 500 kV, or below 345 kV in the case of double-circuit 345-kV lines—100% of costs are allocated using the DFAX method. In August 2015, PJM filed the cost allocation for the Artificial Island Project with FERC in accordance with its transmission tariff (PJM 2015b). Under this method, 50% of the costs for the five high-voltage lines were assigned based on load ratio share, and all remaining costs were assigned based on the DFAX method, including the underwater cable. The resulting cost allocation assigned nearly 98% of the costs to Delmarva Power and Light, which serves customers in Delaware and Maryland. State regulators filed a complaint with FERC, citing the DFAX method results were unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory or preferential (Public Service Electric and Gas Company, Petitioner v. Federal Regulatory Commission 2021). Although FERC originally denied the complaint, it later reversed this decision and, after rehearing, found the cost responsibility assigned by the DFAX method to be unjust and unreasonable for transmission enhancements that address stability-related reliability issues for the broader PJM region. FERC found the beneficiaries of transmission enhancements to solve stability issues are not captured by the DFAX method, which is designed to identify flow-based beneficiaries. 18 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. In March 2020, after years of proceedings and litigation over alternative cost allocation approaches, FERC accepted PJM’s reallocation of costs for the Artificial Island Project using a new stability deviation method. Using the stability deviation method, Delmarva Power and Light was allocated only 13% (PJM 2020) of the project’s costs compared to 98% under the DFAX method. The 230-kV transmission line running under the Delaware River, along with the upgraded substations and new transformer, were completed in fall 2020 with the remaining upgrades completed in spring 2021 (PJM Inside Lines 2021). 3.2.5 ISO New England’s Greater Boston Transmission Project This project illustrates project portfolio planning designed to identify reliability needs and cost allocation based on project costs rather than project benefits. The ISO-NE’s Greater Boston Transmission Project, selected in 2015, is a reliability project consisting of a portfolio of new transmission lines, reconductoring of existing lines, new transformers, and other transmission-related upgrades. The project was identified in the ISO- NE’s Regional System Plan to address numerous thermal and voltage violations and increase transfer capacity into Boston. The final work on an underground 115 kV line was completed in December 2024 and Hudson station work was completed in 2025 was completed in 2025 (ISO- NE 2025b). Although reliability projects are the primary driver for transmission investments across the United States, ISO-NE is notable in that the region has never constructed a transmission project based on economic/system efficiency needs or a public policy goal (ISO-NE 2025b). This is due to a combination of planning rules and methodologies. A report from the External Market Monitor notes that ISO-NE has “aggressive local reliability planning criteria”
